hook.text: The oldest known clothing is 170,000 years old—animal hides sewn with bone needles by early humans in Africa.

buildup.text: Clothing started as survival gear. Humans migrating out of Africa needed covering as temperatures dropped.

discovery.text: Lice DNA reveals clothing's age. Body lice diverged from head lice roughly when humans started wearing clothes.

twist.text: But tropical cultures also dress elaborately despite no cold. Clothing was never just about warmth—it was about meaning.

climax.text: From the first hide to the latest runway, every garment answers the same question: who do I want to be today?

punchline.text: We dressed for identity before we dressed for weather.

quiz.question: How did scientists determine the age of clothing?

details.summary: Before fashion seasons and designer labels, clothing served raw survival needs — warmth, protection, and modesty. Early humans draped animal hides and wove plant fibers, yet even these first garments carried cultural meaning about status, clan, and identity.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding clothing's origins reveals that fashion has always been more than vanity. From the very first garments, what we wear has communicated who we are.
takeaways: Early clothing served survival before style emerged
Even prehistoric garments carried social meaning
The shift from function to fashion was gradual over millennia

faq.question: When did humans first start wearing clothes?
faq.answer: Archaeological and genetic evidence suggests humans began wearing clothes roughly 100,000–170,000 years ago. Lice genetics help date this, since body lice evolved to live in clothing. Early garments were animal hides secured with bone pins.

faq.question: Did early clothing have any decorative purpose?
faq.answer: Yes. Even early garments show signs of dyeing, beadwork, and intentional patterning. Otzi the Iceman's 5,300-year-old outfit combined multiple animal hides in a deliberate design, suggesting aesthetic choices alongside practical needs.
